title: How Should Christians Read Genesis 1? Four Views
subtitle: Four Christian readings of Genesis 1 and 2, each in its own strongest voice. Young-earth, old-earth, evolutionary creation, and the framework view.
triageNote: This is a third-order matter, a question of wisdom and prudence rather than the boundary of the faith. Every view on this page is held by people who confess that God made the heavens and the earth. They confess that Adam's race fell, that the world is a creature and not an accident, and that Jesus rose from the dead. The age of the earth does not appear in a single creed. It was not the issue at Nicaea or Chalcedon. It is not the line between a Christian and an unbeliever. Hold the doctrine of creation, that one good God made all that is out of nothing, as bedrock. Hold the mechanism and the timetable with an open hand. Faithful, Bible-loving believers have read these chapters four different ways for a long time. Lower the temperature. You are arguing with family about the house your Father built, not about whether He built it.
question: Genesis opens with a claim no other ancient book makes plainly. One God, with no rival and no raw material, spoke everything into being and called it good. That much the whole church confesses. The argument is about the next layer down. Genesis 1 sets the work in six days and rests on the seventh. Is it telling us the duration of creation, the age of the world, the order of events as a camera would record them. Or is it doing something else with the days, something an ancient reader would have caught and a modern reader trained on science can miss. How old is the earth. Does it matter to the text. What is the relationship between Adam, formed from dust in Genesis 2, and the long history of life that the rocks and the genomes seem to record. Four serious Christian answers have been given. Each one reads the same two chapters, confesses the same Creator, and struggles honestly with something the others find easier.
whyItMatters:
A teenager raised in church takes a biology class, or watches a documentary, and the floor moves. Either the Bible is true and the textbook is a lie, she is told, or the textbook is true and the Bible is a fairy tale. She is handed a war. She is told to pick a side. The side she picks may decide whether she keeps her faith at all. That false choice has cost the church more young people than almost any doctrine on this site. The Bible never forced that choice on her.

So the first thing that hangs on this is pastoral, not academic. A great deal of damage gets done when a second-order or third-order question gets treated as the gospel itself, so that a young believer thinks losing her view of the age of the earth means losing Christ. It does not. Christians who love the Bible and bow to its authority have read Genesis 1 in at least four serious ways for a very long time. The differences between them are real. They are not the difference between belief and unbelief.

The second thing that hangs on it is how you read. Each view on this page is finally a decision about what kind of literature the opening of Genesis is. That decision shapes everything downstream. Is Genesis 1 a chronicle. An account of material origins in sequence. Is it a polemic against the gods of Egypt and Babylon, dethroning the sun and the sea by making them mere creatures. Is it a temple text, the account of God ordering a cosmos to dwell in. Is it a piece of high literary architecture, framed and patterned to teach rather than to date. You will read the chapter the way your answer tells you to. So it is worth knowing what your answer is, and worth seeing how a faithful Christian could give a different one.

What does not hang on it is your standing before God. That is the reason to discuss it freely. When the stakes are correctly named, you can afford to be honest about the hard parts of your own view, and generous about the strengths of the others. That is exactly the posture this debate has almost never been conducted in.

positions.name: Young-earth creationism
positions.inOneLine: Genesis means what it most plainly says. God created in six ordinary days a few thousand years ago, death entered through Adam's sin, and a global flood reshaped the earth.
positions.bestCase:
Let me start with the word that the whole argument turns on, the Hebrew yom, day. When yom appears with a number, the third day, the sixth day, and when it appears with evening and morning, it means an ordinary day every other place it occurs in the Hebrew Bible. Hundreds of times. Without exception. Moses had words for a long age, olam, dor. He did not use them here. He used day. He numbered it. He bracketed it with evening and morning. I am not importing a wooden literalism onto the text. I am refusing to import a long-age framework that the words themselves resist. The plainest reading of Genesis 1 is the one the church held almost universally until the geology of the early nineteenth century made a long earth fashionable. The pressure to re-read the days came from outside the text, not from inside it.

Now let the rest of Scripture interpret Scripture. In Exodus 20, God grounds the Sabbath command in the six days of creation. Six days you shall labor, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth. The analogy only works if those are the same kind of days your work-week has. The genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 give ages and begettings in a tight chain from Adam. You can argue about gaps. You cannot stretch them into the hundreds of thousands of years that deep time requires without breaking the form. Jesus says that from the beginning of creation God made them male and female. That puts humanity at the beginning, not at the tail end of a four-billion-year process. Paul says death came through one man, Adam, and reigned from Adam onward. That last point is the heart of it. If there were a billion years of predation, disease, and death before Adam, then death is not the wage of sin. It is not the intruder Christ came to destroy. It is simply how God made the world. He called that world very good. I cannot make the cross fit a creation that was a graveyard before any human sinned.

Then there is the flood. Genesis devotes more space to the flood than to the creation itself. It describes a deluge that covered the high mountains, destroyed all flesh, and left a single family alive. The text is not describing a local event in Mesopotamia. The fountains of the great deep burst open. A world ended. Once you take that catastrophe seriously, much of what is offered as evidence for an ancient earth, the layered rock, the fossil graveyards, the vast sedimentary beds, looks instead like exactly what a year-long global catastrophe would leave behind. Laid down fast, not slow. The scientists who founded modern geology assumed slow and steady processes. They had already ruled out a global flood. We are reading the same rocks with a different history in mind.

Let me be honest about what I struggle to explain, because I am asked to be. I will not pretend. Distant starlight is the hardest. If the universe is young, how does light from galaxies billions of light-years away reach us. We have proposed answers, changing light speed, relativistic time effects near a young earth, mature creation. I admit none of them has the settled feel of a solved problem. I hold them as working hypotheses, not as triumphs. The same honesty applies to radiometric dating. I believe it rests on assumptions about constant decay rates and initial conditions that a global catastrophe would overturn. But I cannot simply wave it away. What I will not do is let a difficulty in physics overturn what I take to be the plain teaching of the text and the apostolic doctrine of death through sin. I would rather sit with an unsolved scientific puzzle than re-read Genesis to make peace with a worldview that begins by assuming no flood, no recent creation, and finally no fall.
advocates: Ken Ham (The New Answers Book, Answers in Genesis)
Terry Mortenson (Coming to Grips with Genesis)
Henry M. Morris and John Whitcomb (The Genesis Flood, 1961)
Andrew Snelling (geology)
Douglas Kelly (Creation and Change)

positions.name: Old-earth creation and the day-age reading
positions.inOneLine: The earth is ancient. The rocks and stars indicate exactly that. Genesis 1 records God's real, sequential creative acts over long ages, with the days as epochs or as God's workdays rather than twenty-four-hour periods.
positions.bestCase:
I want to begin where my young-earth brothers and I fully agree, because the agreement is most of the cargo. God created out of nothing. The creation is the deliberate work of a personal God, not an accident. Adam and Eve were real, specially created, the historical head of the human race. The fall was a historical event with cosmic consequences. I deny none of that. What I deny is that faithfulness to Genesis requires me to deny the age of the earth. I do not think the text requires a young earth. I am sure the creation itself does not teach one.

Start with the word day again, because the young-earth case leans its whole weight on it. Yom is a flexible word. Genesis itself proves it. In Genesis 2:4, one verse after the creation week, Moses sums up the entire creation as the day, the yom, in which the Lord made the earth and the heavens. He uses day for the whole creative period. So Moses uses day for a long span in the very same passage. The numbered days and the evening and morning I read as a literary frame for God's successive creative epochs, the day-age reading. Or as God's own workdays, analogous to but not identical with ours, the way Exodus can ground a seven-year sabbath cycle in the seven-day week without the years being days. And notice that the seventh day, God's rest, has no evening and morning closing it. Hebrews 4 treats that seventh day as still open. Still being entered. If the seventh day is a long, ongoing age, the symmetry of the chapter suggests the others may be too.

Then there are the two books. I hold, with a long line of theologians from Augustine to the Princeton divines, that God has written two books, Scripture and nature. Both have the same Author. They cannot finally contradict. The rocks, the radioactive clocks, the expansion of the universe, and the light from distant galaxies all converge on an earth of about four and a half billion years and a universe of about fourteen. I do not treat that convergence as a conspiracy or a deception. I treat it as God's other book, telling me truly how old His world is. To insist on a young earth, I would have to believe one of two things. Either God filled His universe with overwhelming evidence of an age it does not have, which makes Him a deceiver. Or virtually every independent dating method is wrong in the same direction, which strains belief past breaking. The heavens declare the glory of God. The psalm says so. I will let them declare it in the language they actually speak.

What do I struggle with. Honestly, the order. Genesis 1 has light before the sun, vegetation on day three before the sun on day four, and birds before land animals. The fossil order does not match that sequence cleanly. So the day-age reading, which wants the days to track real epochs, has to do real work to harmonize them, treating the sun as becoming visible rather than first existing, and so on. I feel the strain there. I will not pretend the fit is seamless. The harder theological problem I share with everyone who accepts an old earth: animal death before the fall. If the fossil record is largely pre-Adamic, then carnivory and death are older than human sin. I have to argue that the death Paul says came through Adam is specifically human death, spiritual and physical, not the death of every sparrow since the Cambrian. I think that argument is sound. Very good means well-suited to its purpose, not free of all death. But I grant it is the place my view is pressed hardest, and I hold it knowing the cost.
advocates: Hugh Ross (Reasons to Believe; A Matter of Days)
Gleason Archer
Walter Kaiser
C. John Collins (analogical-day view)
the old Princeton tradition (B. B. Warfield was open to an old earth)

positions.name: Evolutionary creation
positions.inOneLine: God created through the long process of evolution, which is His chosen means and not a rival to Him. Genesis 1 teaches who made the world and why, not the biological mechanism of how.
positions.bestCase:
Let me clear away the caricature first, because almost everyone meets this view as a slander before they meet it as a claim. I do not believe the world made itself. I am not a deist who winds the clock and walks away. I am not smuggling atheism into church under a Christian coat. I believe God is the Creator of all things, sovereign over every quark and every mutation. Nothing came to be apart from His will. He is as present and active in the four billion years of life's unfolding as He is in the knitting of a child in the womb, which the psalm describes in the ordinary language of gestation while God is wholly its author. Evolution, on this view, is not an alternative to creation. It is the form God's creating took. The word I would put on it is concursus, the same word the doctrine of providence uses. God works in and through natural causes. Sovereignly, without competing with them.

Now let me say why I read Genesis the way I do. Notice that my reasons are mostly inside the text, not outside it. The opening of Genesis is written against the creation stories of Egypt and Babylon, and it answers their questions, not ours. They asked who is in charge of the cosmos, are the sun and sea and the chaos-monster gods to be feared, where do humans fit. Genesis answers: one God, no rivals, the sun and sea are mere things He made, and humanity is His image-bearing royalty, not the slave-labor of bored deities. That is the freight of the chapter. John Walton has shown, persuasively to me, that Genesis 1 reads like an ancient temple inauguration text. God orders the cosmos as His dwelling and on the seventh day takes up residence to rule. The account is about assigning function and purpose, not about manufacturing material from nothing in sequence. Read that way, the chapter is not even trying to answer the question modern people fight about. It is answering a deeper one, whose world is this and what is it for. It answers magnificently.

What about Adam. This is where I am most often accused of surrender, so let me be careful. Let me concede the difficulty honestly. It is real. The genetic evidence indicates that humanity descends not from a single couple but from a population, never narrowing to two. We share common ancestry with other primates, the broken pseudogenes and shared mutations reading like fingerprints. I take that evidence seriously. It is God's truthful world. So I read Adam and Eve in ways the church has actually entertained before Darwin was born. A real pair God chose and entered into covenant with from among an existing population, the federal and representative head of humanity. Or, with some, a literary and theological Everyman whose story is the true story of us all. I will be honest that this is the hardest knot in my whole position. Paul builds his theology of sin and salvation on Adam as one man, and Luke traces Jesus genealogy back to him. I have to give an account of how the truth Paul is teaching, that sin and death are universal and that they meet their answer in the one man Christ, survives a less literal Adam. I think it does survive, because Paul's argument is finally about the universality of sin and the sufficiency of Christ. But I hold it as the place my view costs the most. I do not wave the cost away.

What do I gain that makes me willing to pay it. A faith that does not have to be at war with the actual world God made. When a believing scientist looks down a microscope and sees the deep history of life written in the genome, I do not need her to disbelieve her eyes to keep her soul. I can tell her that the God of Genesis is the God of that genome too. The long story of life is not an embarrassment to hide but a second scripture to read with wonder. And the cross stands exactly where it always stood, at the center, unmoved by how old the dust was that God breathed into.
advocates: Francis Collins (The Language of God; founder of BioLogos)
John H. Walton (The Lost World of Genesis One)
Denis Alexander
N. T. Wright (on Adam, broadly sympathetic)
the BioLogos Foundation

positions.name: The framework view
positions.inOneLine: Genesis 1 is a carefully structured literary account, arranged by topic rather than chronology. It teaches the fact and the order of God's authority over creation without intending to date the earth or to clock the days.
positions.bestCase:
I want to ask you to do one thing before you decide what Genesis 1 is teaching: actually look at its shape. The shape is the argument, and most readers march straight past it to fight about the calendar. Lay the six days out in two columns. Days one, two, and three are days of forming. They make realms. Day one, light and darkness. Day two, sky and sea. Day three, dry land and vegetation. Days four, five, and six are days of filling, of populating those very realms in the same order. Day four, the lights to rule the day and night, matching day one. Day five, the birds of the sky and fish of the sea, matching day two. Day six, the land animals and humanity on the dry land that grows the vegetation, matching day three. Three realms formed, three realms filled, in exact parallel, and the whole crowned by a seventh day of rest. That is not the structure of a chronicle. That is the structure of a poem. A deliberate literary frame. Once you see it you cannot unsee it.

This is why I say the days are a framework, a literary vessel for the theology, not a timetable. The chapter is arranged thematically, by realm and ruler, not by the clock. The proof is internal. It is not borrowed from any laboratory. Notice that God makes light on day one but does not make the sun, the source of light, until day four. On a strictly sequential reading that is a problem to be solved. On the framework reading it is the design. Day one and day four are the same realm seen first as formed and then as filled, light and then the light-bearers, deliberately paired across the two panels. Notice too that the seventh day, God's rest, has no evening and morning and is never closed. The framework reading expects that. The seventh day is the theological climax, God enthroned over a finished creation, not a twenty-four-hour box. And notice Genesis 2:5, which says no plants had sprung up because God had not yet sent rain and there was no man to work the ground. That explanation assumes ordinary providence, rain and growth and farming, was already operating in the supposed creation week. The verse makes little sense if day three was a single literal day. It makes perfect sense if the days are a frame and not a chronology.

What does this view buy me, and why do I think it is the most honest reading. It lets me take Genesis 1 with total seriousness as the word of God without forcing it to answer a question it never asked. The chapter teaches, with overwhelming clarity, that God alone made everything, that He made it in an ordered and purposeful way, that the creation is good, that humanity is its crown and His image, and that all of it moves toward rest in Him. Those are the things the inspired author labored to teach. They are unshaken by anything geology or biology may discover, because I have not staked them on the age of a rock or the length of a day. I am not at war with the scientists. I am also not bending the text to flatter them, because I am simply not asking the text to settle the scientific question at all. The literary structure gives me that freedom.

Let me name what I struggle with. I owe you that. My view is sometimes accused of being a convenient escape hatch, a way to dodge the science by declaring the chapter non-chronological just when chronology gets inconvenient. I have to answer that the literary structure is really there in the Hebrew. It was noticed by readers, Augustine among them, long before there was any scientific pressure to find it. The harder charge is that by refusing to read the days as sequence, I leave open the questions the other views at least try to answer. The framework view by itself does not tell you whether the earth is young or old, or how Adam relates to natural history. An honest framework reader has to take up those questions on other grounds. I accept that. I am making a claim about what kind of text Genesis 1 is, a claim I think is true and freeing. But it is the beginning of wisdom about origins, not the end of it.
advocates: Meredith G. Kline (Kingdom Prologue; Because It Had Not Rained)
Henri Blocher (In the Beginning)
Bruce Waltke
N. H. Ridderbos (the modern framework's early form)
many Reformed and confessional theologians

biblicalEvidence.passage: Genesis 1:5, the day with evening and morning
biblicalEvidence.summary: And there was evening and there was morning, the first day. This refrain closes six of the days. Young-earth readers note that yom joined to a number and bracketed by evening and morning means an ordinary day everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible. The natural reading is a literal twenty-four-hour day.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for the day-age view. It must read these numbered, evening-and-morning days as long epochs, a sense yom does not otherwise carry when so marked.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The day-age view answers that the chapter's own language is flexible. Genesis 2:4 calls the whole creation the day the Lord made earth and heaven, and evening and morning can frame an epoch as the close of a creative period. The framework view answers that evening and morning belong to the literary structure of the two panels. They mark the rhythm of the poem rather than clocking a literal sunrise, especially since the sun is not made until day four. Evolutionary creation reads the refrain as part of an ancient genre never meant to measure duration at all.

biblicalEvidence.summary: For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and rested the seventh day, therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath. God grounds Israel's work-week in His creation week. Young-earth readers argue the analogy collapses unless the creation days match the ordinary days of human labor.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against the day-age and evolutionary views, since the command seems to equate the creation days with the days a worker keeps.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The analogical-day reading answers that the days are analogous to ours without being identical in length. God's workdays pattern ours the way God's fatherhood patterns human fatherhood without being the same thing. The framework view notes that Exodus draws a theological pattern from Genesis, six and then rest. The pattern holds whether or not the original days were literal. The evolutionary view reads the Sabbath command as resting on the theology of Genesis 1, God's ordering and rest, not on its chronology.

biblicalEvidence.summary: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day the Lord made them, when no bush had yet sprung up because the Lord had not caused it to rain and there was no man to work the ground. The summary calls the whole creation one day. It explains the absence of plants by the ordinary lack of rain and farming.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a strictly sequential reading of day three as one literal day, since this verse assumes ordinary providence, rain and cultivation, was already the operating order.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Young-earth readers take Genesis 2 as a closer account of day six, the making of man. They read verse 5 as describing the specific state of the garden region before Adam, not the globe, so ordinary providence was newly beginning. The day-age view welcomes the verse's use of day for a long span. Evolutionary creation reads chapter 2 as a second, complementary account focused on humanity's vocation, not a chronological appendix to chapter 1.

biblicalEvidence.passage: Genesis 1:14-19, the lights on day four
biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The framework view and evolutionary creation
biblicalEvidence.summary: God makes light on day one but does not make the sun, moon, and stars to give light and mark seasons until day four. The framework view treats this as the design. Day one and day four are the same realm formed then filled, light then light-bearers.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any strictly chronological reading, young-earth or day-age, which must explain a source of light and a day-night cycle for three days before the sun exists.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Young-earth readers answer that God Himself was the light source for the first three days, as He will be again in the new creation where there is no sun. Day four marks the sun being made or appointed to its role. The day-age view often reads day four as the sun becoming visible through a clearing atmosphere rather than first coming into existence. The framework view reads the whole sequence as topical pairing, not chronology, which it regards as the cleaner explanation.

biblicalEvidence.summary: A thousand years in God's sight are as a day that has passed, and with the Lord one day is as a thousand years. Old-earth readers cite these to show that Scripture itself treats God's relation to time as elastic. They warn against pressing the creation days into a human clock.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against the young-earth insistence that day must mean an ordinary day, by showing the Bible's own freedom with the word in relation to God.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Young-earth readers answer that these texts are about God's patience and timelessness, not about the length of the creation days. A simile, a day is like a thousand years, does not redefine the word day in Genesis. The framework view agrees the verses do not date the days and uses them only to caution against literalism. Evolutionary creation reads them as part of the Bible's larger refusal to make God a prisoner of clock-time.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Young-earth creationism, and a challenge to evolutionary creation
biblicalEvidence.summary: Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all are made alive. Paul builds the parallel between the one man Adam and the one man Christ. The young-earth view argues this requires a historical Adam whose sin first introduced death.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for evolutionary creation, which accepts animal death and a human population before any single couple. It must locate the death Paul means in human, not biological, terms, and give an account of Adam as one representative man.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Old-earth creation answers that the death Paul names is specifically human death, the wage of human sin, leaving pre-Adamic animal death untouched. It affirms a historical Adam as federal head. Evolutionary creation argues Paul's point is the universality of sin and the all-sufficiency of Christ, which holds if Adam is the real covenant head of humanity even within a population. It notes Paul's argument turns on the one man Christ being historical, which it fully affirms. The framework view takes no single position here, since it speaks to the genre of Genesis 1, not to Adam's biology.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The waters prevailed and all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered, and all flesh died, and only Noah and those with him remained. Young-earth readers read a global catastrophe that reshaped the earth's geology and laid down much of the fossil record rapidly. That removes the main evidence for deep time.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against old-earth and evolutionary readings, which generally take the flood as historical but regional or as theologically framed. They read the rock and fossil record as the deep history of life rather than the deposit of one year.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Old-earth and evolutionary readers note that all the high mountains and the whole heaven can carry the hyperbolic, universal-from-the-narrator's-horizon sense common in Hebrew narrative. The geology and fossil sequence do not match a single global deposit. And the theological point, judgment and saving grace through the ark, stands whether the flood was global or vast and regional. Young-earth readers reply that the text's scale, the duration, and the ark's purpose all resist a merely local reading. The catastrophe is exactly what the geology should be read in light of.

biblicalEvidence.passage: Mark 10:6 and the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus says that from the beginning of creation God made them male and female, placing humanity at the start. The genealogies chain ages from Adam forward. Young-earth readers add these to argue that Scripture sets humanity near the beginning of a short history, not at the end of a long one.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against old-earth and evolutionary readings, which place humanity very late in a long history and must read the genealogies as selective rather than a continuous chronology.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Old-earth readers note that biblical genealogies are well known to skip generations. To beget can mean to be the ancestor of, so the lists give descent, not a total age of the earth. And from the beginning of creation can mean from the start of the human story Jesus is discussing, marriage, not the first second of the cosmos. Evolutionary creation reads the genealogies as theological and structural, ten names before the flood and ten after, rather than as a chronometer. The framework view, again, takes no stand here, being a claim about the genre of Genesis 1.

weighing:
Here is my own judgment. I want it heard as exactly that, one pastor's reading offered across the table, not a verdict you must accept to stand with me at the Lord's Supper. This is the page where I most want my own hand to be invisible. It is the page where the church has done the most harm by making its hand heavy.

Let me tell you what I am most sure of. It is not a position on the list. The doctrine of creation, that one good God made everything that is out of nothing, freely, and called it good, is bedrock. None of the four views on this page touches it. Every one of them confesses it. The argument is entirely about the mechanism and the timetable. Those are not in the creeds. They were not the issue at the great councils. They are not the line between faith and unbelief. I hold that distinction more firmly than I hold any answer to the age of the earth.

When I read Genesis 1 itself, the framework view persuades me most about what kind of text it is. The two-panel structure, three realms formed and three realms filled, is really there in the Hebrew. Augustine noticed it centuries before any geologist needed it noticed. The light made before the sun, the unclosed seventh day, the ordinary rain and farming assumed in Genesis 2:5, all of it tells me the chapter is teaching the fact and the order of God's authority and the goodness and purpose of His world. It is not handing me a stopwatch. Reading it that way frees me to receive its real freight, which is overwhelming, without staking that freight on a number the text never gives.

What the framework view does not settle, and honestly admits it does not settle, is the age of the earth and the history of Adam. There I lean toward an old earth. Mostly on the two-books conviction. The God who cannot lie wrote the rocks and the stars as well as Genesis. Their testimony to deep time is too convergent and too consistent to be a divine trick. On Adam I hold the line harder. Paul stakes so much on the one man. I cannot follow the path that loosens Adam to a literary figure without feeling the floor of Romans 5 shift under me. But I have brothers I respect who walk it and still preach Christ crucified with all their hearts.

So if you forced me to plant a flag, it would be an old-earth reading governed by a framework understanding of the genre. I would hold a historical Adam as the covenant head of the race. But I plant the flag loosely. The young-earth reader is guarding something precious, the plain authority of the text and the link between death and sin. The evolutionary creationist is guarding something precious too, a faith that need not be at war with the world God actually made. I would not break fellowship over any of it. I would be ashamed to.
charitableDisagreement:
It is tempting to draw this debate as a ladder from most faithful to most compromised, with young-earth at the devout top and evolutionary creation at the slippery bottom. Or to flip the ladder and put young-earth at the embarrassing, anti-science bottom. Both ladders are slanders. Both have driven people out of the church who never needed to leave. Refuse them.

Hear what each side is actually guarding. The young-earth reader is guarding the plain authority of the text against being quietly overruled whenever the culture's science makes a claim, and the link between death and sin that the cross seems to require. These are not small things. The man who holds them is often holding them at real social cost. The old-earth reader is guarding the conviction that God does not deceive, that His creation tells the truth about its own age, and the long Christian tradition that Scripture and nature have one Author and cannot finally clash. The evolutionary creationist is guarding believing scientists, especially the young ones, who should never be told that following the evidence God put in the world is the same as leaving the faith. He is guarding the freedom of a gospel that does not stand or fall on a contested reading of a contested chapter. The framework reader is guarding the text's own literary integrity, the refusal to make Genesis 1 answer a question it was not written to answer.

So is this a hill to die on. No. Say it plainly. Saying it plainly is itself pastoral care. The age of the earth is not in the Apostles Creed or the Nicene Creed. It was not the question at Nicaea or Chalcedon. It is a third-order matter, a question of wisdom about how to read two chapters and how to relate two books. It has room inside a single congregation, even inside a single family, without anyone's salvation being in doubt. Defend the doctrine of creation, that God made all things and made them good, with everything you have. That is the faith. Hold your reading of the days with a much lighter hand, and keep your arm around the believer who counts them differently than you do. The teenager in the biology class is watching how we argue about this. The way we argue is teaching her whether the faith is big enough to hold her questions. Make sure it teaches her yes.

relatedDebates.note: Whether Adam was an individual specially created, the first member of a chosen pair within a population, or a representative literary figure, is the knot where origins meets the doctrine of sin. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 leans on Adam as one man. That is why this is the costliest question for the evolutionary view and the firmest ground for the others.

If the earth is old and the fossil record is largely pre-human, then animal death and predation are older than human sin. Could the very good creation contain animal death. Is the death Paul says entered through Adam specifically human. Those questions are the shared theological pressure point for every old-earth reading.

relatedDebates.topic: The two books and the limits of science
relatedDebates.note: Behind the whole debate stands the question of how Scripture and the natural world, the two books with one Author, are meant to be read together. How much weight should a reading of Genesis give to, or withhold from, the consensus of geology and biology. Where you stand on that prior question quietly decides much of where you land here.

relatedDebates.topic: Concordism and how far to harmonize
relatedDebates.note: Concordism is the project of matching the details of Genesis 1 to the findings of modern science, day by day. The day-age view is concordist by design. The framework and many evolutionary readings deliberately are not, holding that Genesis answers a different kind of question. Whether harmonizing the details honors the text or strains it is its own running argument.
